title: Burst wave decomposition journal
content:
Purpose:
- Investigate how bursty (short, high-amplitude) waves of requests interact with adaptive batching and prefix KV caching. Goal: isolate the components that inflate p99 during a burst and validate an inexpensive heuristic to lower tail without harming steady-state throughput.

Hypotheses:
1) A short, high-QPS burst causes two orthogonal tail contributors: queueing/backpressure at the ingress and cache-miss-driven kernel penalties (KV load + cold attention kernels).
2) Adaptive batch windowing that tightens quickly on burst onset (reduce window to 2–4ms) will reduce enqueue tail but may increase GPU kernel overhead if it causes many small kernels; combining with quick cache-priming reduces p99 overall.
3) A lightweight burst detector (exponential CUSUM on rolling 100ms QPS) can flip batching and routing policy fast enough to matter.

Environment / versions:
- Model: rw-13b-q4f16 (quantized variant we use for staging)
- Runtime: redwood-runtime v1.8.0 (fused_attention_v2, continuous-batching opt on)
- Serving nodes: 4x A100-80GB (nvidia), Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15
- Client: redwood-loadbench v0.9.1 (custom arrival script)
- Network: colocated in us-west1 (same DC), measured baseline RTT ~0.8ms

Load profile used (synth):
- Background steady: 50 QPS (1k tokens/sec average requests)
- Burst wave: every 60s inject a 4s burst, peak QPS ~600, shaped triangular (build 1s upslope, 2s plateau, 1s downslope)
- 10 bursts / run (~10 minutes total)
- Payload: prompt length ~64 tokens, generation target 128 tokens (sampling, temp 0.7)

Configs compared:
A) baseline-static: max_batch = 64, batch_window = 8ms, no adaptive behavior, no explicit cache prefill.
B) adaptive-fast: adaptive window 2–40ms (start small on new tenant traffic, grow opportunistically), burst-detector enabled to clamp window to 2ms within 120ms of detection.
C) adaptive-fast + cache-primed: same as B but on detector hit we prefetch top-8 prefix keys for common tenant prompts (prefill KV cache via background warm RPC).

Commands (client):
- Launch generator: ./redwood-loadbench --arrival-pattern burst-triangular --background 50 --burst-peak 600 --burst-duration 4 --cycle 60 --requests 60000 --concurrency 400
- Runtime flags (node): RUNTIME_FLAGS="--batch-window-default=8ms --adaptive-batching=true --burst-detector=true" systemctl restart redwood-runtime

Observables captured per request (traced):
- ingress_enqueue_ms (time waiting in request queue before batch formation)
- batch_wait_ms (time batch window held open for more requests)
- kv_load_ms (time spent reading KV cache from host to GPU)
- kernel_exec_ms (GPU execution time)
- post_encode_ms (serialization / network send back)
- node_gpu_util (averaged sample)
- kv_hit (boolean)

Representative CSV snippet (header on first line, then sample rows)
- header: timestamp, qps, ingress_enqueue_ms, batch_wait_ms, kv_load_ms, kernel_exec_ms, post_encode_ms, kv_hit
- sample rows:
2025-02-12T18:02:11.142Z, 48, 0.3, 4.6, 0.8, 72.1, 1.2, true
2025-02-12T18:02:30.781Z, 610, 12.4, 7.9, 13.2, 80.0, 2.4, false
2025-02-12T18:02:31.092Z, 598, 2.1, 2.0, 1.1, 74.6, 1.8, true

Summary results (aggregated per run):
- Metric convention: latencies in ms, throughput in req/s, token throughput in tokens/s

A) baseline-static:
- steady-state (outside bursts): p50=85, p95=140, p99=240, throughput stable at 48 req/s per node, GPU util ~62%
- during burst: observed p50=110, p95=420, p99=950 (several ~1s+ outliers), queuing dominated: mean ingress_enqueue_ms spiked to 28ms, but also many kv_load_ms spikes to 20–80ms for cold prompts. KV hit rate dropped to 12% at burst peak.

B) adaptive-fast:
- steady-state: p50=88, p95=150, p99=260 (slightly worse p95 than baseline due to more aggressive small-batch kernels), throughput similar, GPU util ~60% (lower transiently).
- during burst: p50=94, p95=220, p99=470 — big improvement vs baseline p99 (950 -> 470). Ingress_enqueue_ms median fell from 28ms to 6.2ms at peak. However kernel_exec_ms variance increased; more small kernels ran but usually <15ms.

C) adaptive-fast + cache-primed:
- steady-state: p50=87, p95=145, p99=255.
- during burst: p50=90, p95=190, p99=320. KV hit rate at burst peak improved to ~55% because prefetch warmed common prefixes in <40ms. Combined effect: both enqueue and kv penalties reduced; overall p99 reduced ~66% vs baseline.

Tail decomposition (percent contribution to p99 observed during burst peak):
- baseline: enqueue/backpressure 48%, kv-load 28%, kernel_exec 15%, serialization+others 9%
- adaptive-fast: enqueue 18%, kv-load 34%, kernel_exec 36%, others 12%
- adaptive+prime: enqueue 12%, kv-load 20%, kernel_exec 44%, others 14%
Notes: kernel_exec fraction rises in adaptive configs because we reduced queueing and KV stalls so remaining tail is more purely GPU execution variance (quantization/attention path coldstarts).

Quick conclusions / takeaways:
- Adaptive batch window + fast detector materially reduces enqueue/backpressure tail and lowers p99 significantly vs a static conservative window.
- Doing adaptive batching alone shifts the tail to kernel variance; without cache warmup you trade queueing tail for more numerous small kernels (but overall tail still improves).
- A cheap prefix prefetch on detector hit yields outsized wins: it cuts kv-miss spikes and complements adaptive batching to produce the best p99/throughput trade-off of the three configs.
- Detector thresholds matter: too-aggressive detection flips into micro-batching too often and costs throughput; tuned CUSUM with minimum dwell 120ms worked well in these runs.

Open questions / next experiments:
1) Kernel amortization strategies: can we fuse tiny kernels caused by adaptive batching into batched micro-batches in the runtime without reintroducing queueing? Prototype idea: group multiple small windows into a single GPU batch if they arrive within 6ms but avoid waiting longer than 12ms.
2) Prefetch scope: prefetching top-8 prefixes helped for our prompt mix; measure sensitivity to prompt entropy (highly custom prompts see diminished benefit). Run experiments with randomized user prompts and real production prompt corpus sample.
3) Multi-tenant fairness: when bursts come from a single tenant vs many tenants, routing + prefetch budget should be tenant-aware. Need fairness experiments and quota guardrails to avoid noisy-tenant hogging.
4) Cost model: quantify added background prefetch traffic vs saved tokens/GPU time to ensure cost-positive.

Action items (short):
- [ ] Share this note with Samir / runtime team; ask for micro-fusion feasibility (ticketed as RINF-6783).
- [ ] Run randomized prompt corpus sweep (10 runs) with adaptive+prefetch, collect KV hit heatmap (owner: Rui).
- [ ] Add a telemetry field for burst_detector_state to logs to better align traces to detection windows (owner: Clara).
- [ ] Validate on rw-70b-INT8 staging cluster — larger model might change kernel fraction dramatically.

Appendix: quick trace pattern to look for in future runs:
- Pattern A (queuing tail): ingress_enqueue_ms rising correlated with small batch sizes and high per-node queue depth.
- Pattern B (kv penalty): kv_load_ms spikes >20ms coincident with kv_hit=false, often followed by kernel_exec_ms spike (cache miss leads to GPU path change).
- Pattern C (kernel variance): steady ingress, kv_hit=true but kernel_exec_ms shows heavy long tail (likely kernel cold paths, quantization path jitter).

Notes to self (things I scribbled while running):
- Detector dwell 120ms tuned by eyeballing: lower => toggles too often (esp. in sawtooth microbursts), higher => late flips.
- Prefetch noise: keep prefetch budget < 2% of steady-state bandwidth to avoid overloading routers during large fleet-wide bursts.
- Remember to annotate runs with git commit SHA and runtime flags (made mistakes in earlier runs).

End of journal entry.

-- Clara
